title: The bondage of sin leaves the sinner free in sinning
source_text: LVI. Praeterea satis manifestum fecimus, Protestantes docere quidem in statu naturae lapsae, hominem sine gratia esse peccati servum, & veluti captivum: sed illam tamen peccati servitutem, secundum ipsos, non obstare, quominus libere in peccatum feratur, & bonum lege praeceptum aversetur & omittat; ac in eo Arbitrii sui libertatem plene exerceat; cum id faciat non coactus, & ex rationis corruptae deliberato judicio, ac quum hoc aut illud peccatum committit, potestatem habeat ab eo abstinendi.
pass_a_gloss: LVI. Moreover we made sufficiently manifest, that the Protestants teach indeed that in the state of fallen nature, man without grace is the servant of sin, and as it were captive: but that that servitude of sin, according to them, does not prevent that freely he be borne into sin, and turn away from and omit the good commanded by the law; and in this fully exercise the liberty of his Choice; since he does it not compelled, and from the deliberate judgement of corrupt reason, and when he commits this or that sin, he has the power of abstaining from it.
pass_b_english: Thesis LVI. We have also shown clearly enough that the Protestants teach that in the state of fallen nature man without grace is the slave of sin and a kind of captive. On their view, though, this bondage to sin does not prevent him from being carried freely into sin, and from turning away from and neglecting the good the law commands.

In this he fully exercises the freedom of his choice, since he acts without compulsion and from the deliberate judgement of a corrupt reason, and when he commits this sin or that one, he has the power to refrain from it.

choices.why: The freedom from coercion and from brute natural determination that belongs to every agent with intellect and will, which sin does not remove.
